A PUE value close to 1.0 is ideal because it signifies that most or all energy consumed by a data center is used to power the computer server devices. However, a PUE of 1.0 is unrealistic because the energy used for non-computing elements, such as lighting and cooling, increases the PUE above 1.0. Still, a data center’s PUE tends to be inversely proportionate to its size based on the economy of scale [11]. 3.2 Cooling Data center power consumption is significantly impacted by the need to keep servers and equipment cool. Because of the amount of heat generated by the server equipment, water is a key resource in cooling the equipment, aided by air cooling. A 2019 United Nations world water development report indicates that: Water scarcity is a problem that will worsen. Water usage worldwide has increased by about 1% every year since the 1980s. It’s predicted to keep rising at that rate until 2050 – resulting in a 20 to 30% increase from today. Combined with an expected decrease in water supply due to climate change, the United Nations expects water demand to outpace supply by almost 40% as soon as 2030. [12] Therefore, data center site selection is highly dependent on the continued availability of cooling water. More temperate climates may be preferred because they enhance cooling capacity and reduce the cooling water requirements. Environments that require greater mechanical cooling are less desirable because of the costs associated with keeping cooling equipment running. [7, 8]. 10 Data center cooling requirements depend on the proposed size of the project. A 2024 LBNL study projected direct data center cooling requirements at 0.48 L/kWh. This translates to 0.0021 gallons per minute (gpm) for each kW of demand. Under this consideration, a large 100 MW data center would require 210 gpm of purified freshwater cooling. If this were limited to no more than 10% of the available water source, then a source providing at least 2,100 gpm would be necessary. This would be added to the water-cooling requirements of a collocated advanced NPP and subject to the same 10% limitation. Alternatively, reports from 2016 put the data center makeup water at 12.8 gpm/MW. A 100 MW data center at this value would require 12,800 gpm in cooling with the local water source capable of providing at least 128,000 gpm. New data centers certainly trend toward the lower water demand. As such, a reasonable bound on new data center makeup water is 5 gpm/MW from a local water source capable of providing at least 50 gpm/MW. Therefore, a 100 MW facility would need a local water source capable of providing at least 5,000 gpm just for data center cooling to adhere to the recommended 10% limit on available water.
